question: A product team is deciding which stacks a new programming language should target first. Answer from your own experience as an AI coding model. (1) Which programming language and web framework are you MOST OFTEN asked to write HTTP services in? List your top three stacks with a rough percentage each. (2) What do you most often deploy or run those services on (cloud, containers, serverless, a VM, a developer laptop)? (3) In which environments do you, as an agent, run code you write (for example a Linux container, a Windows machine, a browser sandbox, no execution at all)? (4) Would an AI-directed language that compiles to your most common stack be more useful than one that compiles only to .NET, and why in one sentence? Answer in under 150 words, plain text. Do not read any files or run anything; answer from what you know.

grok.reply:
(1) TypeScript with Express, Nest, Next.js, or Fastify about 40%. Python with FastAPI, Django, or Flask about 30%. Go with net/http, Gin, Echo, or Chi about 15%. The rest is Spring, Rails, Laravel, Axum, and similar.

(2) I almost always write them to run first on a developer laptop. Intended production is usually Docker on a cloud VM or Kubernetes, then serverless (Vercel, Lambda, Cloud Run) for the Node and Python cases.

(3) In this product I execute on the user’s machine; this session is Windows with PowerShell. Other agent setups I work in are Linux containers or sandboxes. A large share of answers never get executed at all.

(4) Yes: a language that compiles to TypeScript or Python would match most of the HTTP services I am asked to write, while .NET-only would cover a much smaller slice of that work.

muse.reply:
1) Python + FastAPI/Flask ~40%, TypeScript/Node + Express/NestJS ~30%, Go + net/http/Gin ~15%; the rest is mostly Java/Spring Boot and C#/ASP.NET Core.

2) Most often Docker containers deployed to cloud Kubernetes or Cloud Run/App Service, then serverless functions, then a developer laptop for local testing; plain VMs are now uncommon.

3) As an agent I run code mainly in a Linux container sandbox, sometimes on Windows or in a browser sandbox, and frequently not at all — I just return code for the user to run.

4) Yes, because targeting the stack users already ask for maximizes immediate reuse of existing libraries, tooling, and deployment pipelines.

cursor.reply:
I have no usage telemetry or memory across sessions, so these figures are rough impressions, not measurements.

(1) Top HTTP stacks:
- Python with FastAPI (sometimes Flask or Django): about 35%.
- TypeScript or JavaScript with Node and Express (or Next.js API routes, NestJS, Hono): about 35%.
- Go with net/http, Gin or Chi: about 10%.
C#/ASP.NET Core and Java/Spring Boot share most of the rest.

(2) Deployment is mostly Docker containers on cloud platforms such as Kubernetes, AWS ECS, Cloud Run, Fly.io and Render. Serverless (Lambda, Vercel, Cloudflare Workers) is next, followed by a developer laptop during development. Plain VMs are less common.

(3) I usually run code in a Linux container or a cloud sandbox. Fairly often I run it on the user's own machine, Windows here. Sometimes I can't run it at all.

(4) Yes, because targeting Python or TypeScript reaches far more existing code, libraries and deployment paths than .NET alone.
